Default Priors of the Hierarchical Bayes Models

Source: vignettes/hb-priors.Rmd
hb-priors.Rmd

hb_area(), hb_unit() and hb_twofold() fit their models with INLA (inla_engine(), the default) or with NUTS in NumPyro (jax_engine()). Both engines use the same default priors, so a model gives the same estimates whichever engine fits it. This article lists those priors, explains why they were chosen and summarises the simulations behind them.

With few areas, or with one observation per area, the prior of a variance or dispersion parameter is not a technicality: the data hardly inform it, and its prior decides how much the estimates are shrunk and how wide the intervals are.

The models at a glance

The three functions fit generalised linear mixed models. Written out with their default priors, where ss is the scale of the standard deviations: s=sd(y)s = \mathrm{sd}(y) for Gaussian models (the standard deviation of the direct estimates, or of the unit responses for hb_unit()) and s=1s = 1 on the logit or log scale of the other families.

Area level, hb_area(). For area dd (and period tt in a panel),

yd∣μd∼f(μd,ψd),g(μd)=xd⊤β+ud[+γt+δdt][+log⁡Ed],y_d \mid \mu_d \sim f(\mu_d, \psi_d), \qquad g(\mu_d) = x_d^\top \beta + u_d \; [+\, \gamma_t + \delta_{dt}] \; [+\, \log E_d],

with the likelihood ff, its dispersion ψd\psi_d and the link gg set by family (see Priors of the likelihood), and

Term Argument Model Default prior
β\beta formula fixed effects intercept flat; others N(0,1000)N(0, 1000)
udu_d spatial = "none" iid N(0,σu2)N(0, \sigma_u^2) σu∼\sigma_u \sim half-normal(s)(s)
"besag" intrinsic CAR (ICAR) on the graph of W, scaled σu∼\sigma_u \sim half-normal(s)(s)
"bym" iid + ICAR, each with its own SD both SDs half-normal(s)(s)
"bym2" σu(1−ϕvd+ϕud*)\sigma_u(\sqrt{1 - \phi}\, v_d + \sqrt{\phi}\, u^*_d), u*u^* a scaled ICAR σu∼\sigma_u \sim half-normal(s)(s); PC prior P(ϕ<0.5)=0.5P(\phi < 0.5) = 0.5
"leroux" precision σu−2{(1−λ)I+λR}\sigma_u^{-2}\{(1 - \lambda) I + \lambda R\}, RR the ICAR structure σu∼\sigma_u \sim half-normal(s)(s); λ∼\lambda \sim Uniform(0,1)(0, 1)
"sar" u=(I−ρW)−1εu = (I - \rho W)^{-1} \varepsilon, εd∼N(0,σu2)\varepsilon_d \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) σu∼\sigma_u \sim half-normal(s)(s); ρ∼\rho \sim Uniform(−0.999,0.999)(-0.999, 0.999)
"slm" η=(I−ρW)−1(Xβ+ε)\eta = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X\beta + \varepsilon) σu∼\sigma_u \sim half-normal(s)(s); ρ\rho uniform on the range allowed by the eigenvalues of W
γt\gamma_t temporal "rw1", "rw2", "ar1" or "iid" σγ∼\sigma_\gamma \sim half-normal(s)(s); AR(1): N(0,1/0.15)N(0, 1/0.15) on log⁡{(1+ρ)/(1−ρ)}\log\{(1 + \rho)/(1 - \rho)\}
δdt\delta_{dt} st_interaction domain-specific trends, a separable field or Knorr-Held types I-IV its SD half-normal(s)(s); AR(1) correlation as for γt\gamma_t

Unit level, hb_unit(). For unit jj in domain dd,

ydj∣μdj∼f(μdj),g(μdj)=xdj⊤β+ud,y_{dj} \mid \mu_{dj} \sim f(\mu_{dj}), \qquad g(\mu_{dj}) = x_{dj}^\top \beta + u_d,

with ff normal (edj∼N(0,σe2)e_{dj} \sim N(0, \sigma_e^2), σe∼\sigma_e \sim half-normal(s)(s)), Bernoulli or Poisson, udu_d iid, Besag or BYM2 with the priors above, and the target the population mean of domain dd, computed from the population means of the covariates in Xpop.

Sub-area level, hb_twofold(). For sub-area jj in area ii,

yij∣μij∼f(μij),g(μij)=xij⊤β+vi+uij,y_{ij} \mid \mu_{ij} \sim f(\mu_{ij}), \qquad g(\mu_{ij}) = x_{ij}^\top \beta + v_i + u_{ij},

with ff normal with the known sampling variance VijV_{ij}, binomial or Poisson, viv_i iid, Besag or BYM2 and uiju_{ij} iid; both SDs have half-normal(s)(s) priors, with ss from the sub-area direct estimates. The area targets aggregate the sub-area means with the weights in weight.

All intrinsic models (Besag, BYM, BYM2 and the random walks) are scaled (scale_model = TRUE) so that σ\sigma is a typical marginal standard deviation whatever the graph, which is what makes one prior scale sensible for all of them (Sørbye and Rue 2014).

Priors of the model parameters

Parameter Default (inla_engine(), jax_engine(priors = "inla")) jax_engine(priors = "weakly_informative")
Random-effect SD σ\sigma (area, sub-area, time, area-by-time) Half-normal(s)(s): s=sd(y)s = \mathrm{sd}(y) for Gaussian models, s=1s = 1 on the link scale otherwise Half-normal(1)(1) on the standardised response or the link scale
BYM2 mixing parameter ϕ\phi PC prior with P(ϕ<0.5)=0.5P(\phi < 0.5) = 0.5 Uniform(0,1)(0, 1)
AR(1) correlation ρ\rho N(0,1/0.15)N(0, 1/0.15) on log⁡{(1+ρ)/(1−ρ)}\log\{(1 + \rho)/(1 - \rho)\} Uniform(−1,1)(-1, 1)
Leroux λ\lambda, SAR ρ\rho Uniform Uniform
Coefficients β\beta N(0,1000)N(0, 1000); intercept flat (INLA) or nearly flat (JAX) N(0,102)N(0, 10^2) on the standardised scale (N(0,2.52)N(0, 2.5^2) for logit links)

Here sd(y)\mathrm{sd}(y) is the standard deviation of the observed direct estimates (of the unit responses for hb_unit()). With benchmark_method = "wfq" the coefficients get nearly flat priors (N(0,106)N(0, 10^6), intercept N(0,104)N(0, 10^4)) instead, so that the benchmarking covariate is not shrunk. inla_engine() writes the half-normal prior as an expression: prior on the log precision θ=−2log⁡σ\theta = -2 \log \sigma, so that INLA and NumPyro use the same density.

jax_engine() has two priors that INLA does not have. With robust = TRUE the random effects are Student-tt with degrees of freedom ν∼\nu \sim Uniform(2.5,30)(2.5, 30). With prior_beta = "horseshoe" the coefficients get a regularised horseshoe prior (Piironen and Vehtari 2017): local scales λj∼C+(1)\lambda_j \sim C^+(1), global scale τ∼C+(1)\tau \sim C^+(1) and slab c2∼c^2 \sim Inv-Gamma(2,8)(2, 8).

Priors of the likelihood

Parameter When Prior

Beta precision vardir given Fixed per area at μ̂d(1−μ̂d)/Vd−1\hat\mu_d(1 - \hat\mu_d)/V_d - 1, with μ̂d\hat\mu_d from a first fit
Beta precision trials given (no vardir) Fixed per area at nd−1n_d - 1
Negative binomial size vardir given Fixed per area at μ̂d2/(Vd−μ̂d)\hat\mu_d^2 / (V_d - \hat\mu_d), with μ̂d\hat\mu_d from a first fit

Negative binomial size no vardir Half-normal(10)(10), both engines
Gaussian residual SD no vardir (and the unit errors of hb_unit()) Half-normal(sd(y))(\mathrm{sd}(y)), both engines
Beta precision ϕ\phi no vardir, no trials Log-gamma(1,0.1)(1, 0.1) on log⁡ϕ\log\phi, i.e. ϕ∼\phi \sim Exponential(0.1)(0.1), both engines (half-normal(10)(10) with jax_engine(priors = "weakly_informative"))

Why half-normal standard deviations

INLA’s penalised complexity (PC) prior on an SD, P(σ>U)=αP(\sigma > U) = \alpha, is a good default when UU is chosen for the problem (Simpson et al. 2017). The common choice U=1U = 1, α=0.01\alpha = 0.01 is not: it is tied to the unit of the response. On the mys data, the REML estimate of the area SD is 1.62 and sd(y)=2.21\mathrm{sd}(y) = 2.21, but PC(1,0.01)(1, 0.01) gives P(σ>1.62)=0.0006P(\sigma > 1.62) = 0.0006, and the prior shrinks the area effects far more than the data suggest. In a Fay-Herriot simulation (30 areas) the 95% intervals under PC(1,0.01)(1, 0.01) covered 94%, 85% and 38% of the true means with the same data in three units (y times 0.1, 1 and 10).

Scaling the prior to the response removes the dependence on the unit. Among the scaled priors, the half-normal covered as the EBLUP intervals, while the PC priors, which put much mass near σ=0\sigma = 0, still shrank the area SD (benchmarks/validation/default_sd_prior.R; 150 replicates, known vardir):

Areas Area SD EBLUP Half-normal(sdy)(\mathrm{sd}\,y) PC, α=0.01\alpha = 0.01 PC, α=0.05\alpha = 0.05
15 0.4 0.960 0.966 0.917 0.942
30 0.4 0.940 0.958 0.905 0.929
60 0.4 0.927 0.943 0.898 0.918
15 0.8 0.930 0.932 0.853 0.890
30 0.8 0.934 0.929 0.888 0.909
60 0.8 0.942 0.939 0.919 0.928

For models with a link function the random effects are on the logit or log scale, where an SD of 1 is already large, so the scale is 1. Against PC(1,0.01)(1, 0.01) and half-normal(2.5)(2.5) (the default of tipsae), half-normal(1)(1) covered at least as well, and it estimated the area SD with less bias (default_sd_prior_glm.R, default_sd_prior_glm_more.R; mean coverage over the scenarios, worst scenario in brackets):

Response Half-normal(1)(1) Half-normal(2.5)(2.5) PC(1,0.01)(1, 0.01)
Binomial, ndn_d 20-200 0.927-0.950 0.927-0.952 0.918-0.944
Binomial, ndn_d 5-20 0.950 (0.932) 0.953 (0.938) 0.919 (0.864)
Beta, ndn_d 5-20 0.938 (0.925) 0.940 (0.929) 0.908 (0.873)
Poisson 0.947 (0.944) 0.948 (0.944) 0.943 (0.934)
Binomial BYM2 0.947 (0.941) 0.947 (0.942) 0.942 (0.934)

The half-normal prior is also the weakly informative choice of Gelman (2006) for hierarchical SDs. It suits NUTS better than INLA’s vague log-gamma prior on the precision, whose ridge towards σ=0\sigma = 0 slows the sampler down.

The BYM2 and AR(1) priors are INLA’s defaults (Riebler et al. 2016), reproduced in JAX: jax_engine() evaluates the PC density of ϕ\phi from the eigenvalues of the scaled ICAR precision, as INLA:::inla.pc.bym.phi() does. With these priors the two engines agree on mys within 0.03 (iid) and 0.05 (BYM2) posterior SD.

Dispersion with one observation per area

In an area-level model each area contributes one direct estimate. For the gamma and negative binomial likelihoods the variance of that estimate depends on a dispersion parameter as well as on the area effect:

  • gamma: CV2≈1/shape+σ2\mathrm{CV}^2 \approx 1/\text{shape} + \sigma^2;
  • negative binomial: Var≈μ+μ2/size+μ2(eσ2−1)\mathrm{Var} \approx \mu + \mu^2/\text{size} + \mu^2(e^{\sigma^2} - 1).

With one observation per area the data identify only the sum, so the dispersion follows its prior. INLA’s own defaults favour little sampling noise: log-gamma(1,0.01)(1, 0.01) on the gamma precision and pc.mgamma(7)(7) on the size, which shrinks towards Poisson. They put the estimate at 76-84 (gamma) and 110-180 (size) whatever the truth, and the intervals then missed the true means when the sampling noise was real. Both engines therefore use a half-normal(10)(10) prior on the gamma precision and on the size. Coverage of 95% intervals, sampled areas, area SD 0.3 / 0.8 (gamma_shape_prior.R, nb_size_prior.R; 30 areas, 100 replicates):

Likelihood True dispersion Half-normal(10)(10) INLA’s default
Gamma shape 5 0.930 / 0.925 0.593 / 0.522
Gamma shape 20 0.959 / 0.986 0.862 / 0.826
Gamma shape 100 0.950 / 0.999 0.979 / 0.993
Negative binomial size 3 0.928 / 0.896 0.816 / 0.756
Negative binomial size 10 0.949 / 0.965 0.913 / 0.915
Negative binomial size 100 0.939 / 0.990 0.965 / 0.980

The half-normal(10)(10) prior has a cost: when the sampling noise is small (shape or size 100) its intervals are too wide and its errors larger. hb_area() therefore warns when a gamma or negative binomial model is fitted without vardir. The sampling variances fix the dispersion of each area and give 92-94% (gamma) and 91-95% (negative binomial) coverage (dispersion_vardir.R). A Poisson model is not an alternative for overdispersed counts: it ignores the overdispersion and covered 68-75%.

The Gaussian and beta likelihoods have the same problem without vardir. For the Gaussian residual SD, INLA’s own default, log-gamma(1,5×10−5)(1, 5 \times 10^{-5}) on the precision, is disastrous here: it put the residual SD near zero (precision about 1.5×1041.5 \times 10^4), the area means collapsed onto the direct estimates and their intervals covered almost none of the true means. The half-normal prior with the scale of the response, the prior of the area SD, covered nominally in every unit of the response (likelihood_priors.R; 30 areas, 60 replicates, coverage of 95% intervals for sampled areas, yy in its unit / times 10):

Area SD Residual SD Half-normal(sdy)(\mathrm{sd}\,y) INLA’s default
0.5 0.5 0.943 / 0.943 0.038 / 0.006
0.5 1 0.949 / 0.947 0.024 / 0.001
1 0.5 0.955 / 0.968 0.033 / 0.003
1 1 0.953 / 0.938 0.019 / 0.002

For the beta precision, INLA’s default log-gamma(1,0.1)(1, 0.1) covered as well as half-normal(10)(10) or better (area SD 0.3 / 0.8):

True ϕ\phi Log-gamma(1,0.1)(1, 0.1) Half-normal(10)(10)
10 0.960 / 0.937 0.965 / 0.938
50 0.931 / 0.903 0.913 / 0.869
200 0.875 / 0.925 0.841 / 0.871

so both engines use it. Neither prior covers well when the sampling noise is small (ϕ=200\phi = 200), and the areas without a direct estimate then covered only 73-80%; give vardir or trials when they are known.

Beta precision from vardir

The beta variance is μd(1−μd)/(ϕd+1)\mu_d(1 - \mu_d)/(\phi_d + 1), so a known sampling variance fixes ϕd=μd(1−μd)/Vd−1\phi_d = \mu_d(1 - \mu_d)/V_d - 1 at the unknown true proportion. Putting the direct estimate ydy_d in place of μd\mu_d (Janicki 2020) gives the model a sampling variance of Vdμd(1−μd)/{yd(1−yd)}V_d\,\mu_d(1 - \mu_d)/\{y_d(1 - y_d)\} instead of VdV_d, too small wherever ydy_d happens to fall far from μd\mu_d. hb_area() therefore fits the model twice and takes ϕd\phi_d at the posterior mean of the first fit. tipsae (type_disp = "var") instead lets ϕd\phi_d follow the model mean inside the MCMC; that keeps the variance at VdV_d exactly, but a low mean then also lowers the precision, which gives the likelihood a second mode near 0. Coverage of 95% intervals for sampled areas, area SD 0.3 / 0.8 (beta_vardir_phi.R; 30 areas, 60 replicates, VdV_d the true sampling variance):

Proportions near Direct estimate Two stages tipsae True ϕd\phi_d
0.08 0.844 / 0.812 0.938 / 0.896 0.938 / 0.931 0.953 / 0.918
0.23 0.922 / 0.931 0.948 / 0.933 0.951 / 0.954 0.950 / 0.944

tipsae covered as well, but 11 of its 240 fits did not converge (R-hat up to 8.7).

Checking the priors of a fit

The priors that INLA actually used, including any given in inla_engine(), are listed by INLA::inla.priors.used(). The half-normal priors appear as expression: priors on the log precision, with their scale ss written out:

fit <- hb_area(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = mys, vardir = "vardir")
INLA::inla.priors.used(fit$fit)
#> section=[random]
#>   tag=[..domain_id..] component=[..domain_id..]
#>     theta1:
#>       parameter=[log precision]
#>       prior=[expression: s = 2.20822220299071; sigma = exp(-theta/2); ...]

print(fit$engine_spec) shows the engine settings, and for jax_engine() the prior set ("inla" or "weakly_informative").

When to change a prior

The defaults are meant to be safe without tuning, not to encode knowledge of a particular survey. Consider changing them when

  • you have real prior knowledge of the variation between areas. A PC prior P(σu>U)=αP(\sigma_u > U) = \alpha with UU the largest plausible area SD in the unit of the response (or on the link scale) states this directly; see the first example below.
  • the areas differ a lot on the link scale. Half-normal(1)(1) gives P(σu>2)=0.046P(\sigma_u > 2) = 0.046; if logit- or log-scale area effects with an SD above 2 are plausible, raise the scale.
  • a dispersion parameter follows its prior. Without vardir (or trials) the dispersion of the gamma, negative binomial and beta likelihoods is weakly identified, and the intervals depend on its prior. Giving the sampling variances is better than tuning that prior.

With few areas, refit with a second prior and compare the estimates in df_hb: if they move by a sizeable fraction of their posterior SD, report the sensitivity.

Changing the priors

inla_engine() takes INLA prior specifications for every hyperparameter. A prior given there replaces the default.

library(fastsae)
data("mys")

# PC prior on the area SD instead of the half-normal default
fit <- hb_area(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  data = mys, vardir = "vardir",
  engine = inla_engine(prior_prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))
)

# INLA's own prior on the negative binomial size (d: counts y, covariate x, exposure E)
fit_nb <- hb_area(y ~ x,
  data = d, family = "nbinomial", exposure = "E",
  engine = inla_engine(control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(prior = "pc.mgamma", param = 7))))
)

The other arguments are prior_phi (BYM2), prior_rho (Leroux, SAR, SLM), prior_prec_time and prior_rho_time (temporal effect) and prior_prec_subarea (hb_twofold()). jax_engine() offers the two prior sets of the first table:

fit_jax <- hb_area(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  data = mys, vardir = "vardir",
  engine = jax_engine(priors = "weakly_informative")
)

References

  • Gelman, A. (2006). Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models. Bayesian Analysis, 1(3), 515-534.
  • Janicki, R. (2020). Properties of the beta regression model for small area estimation of proportions and application to estimation of poverty rates. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 49(9), 2264-2284.
  • Piironen, J. and Vehtari, A. (2017). Sparsity information and regularization in the horseshoe and other shrinkage priors. Electronic Journal of Statistics, 11(2), 5018-5051.
  • Riebler, A., Sørbye, S. H., Simpson, D. and Rue, H. (2016). An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 25(4), 1145-1165.
  • Simpson, D., Rue, H., Riebler, A., Martins, T. G. and Sørbye, S. H. (2017). Penalising model component complexity: a principled approach to constructing priors. Statistical Science, 32(1), 1-28.
  • Sørbye, S. H. and Rue, H. (2014). Scaling intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field priors in spatial modelling. Spatial Statistics, 8, 39-51.
